claims.text: The baseline refractory high-entropy alloy, exemplified by WNbMoTaTi, has a primary BCC structure.
The untreated baseline exhibits high strength.
The untreated baseline exhibits high impact-induced energy release.
The untreated baseline has limited ductility and nonuniform deformation.
Adding approximately 0.5–2 wt.% Zr and applying a controlled heat treatment will produce nanometer-scale Zr-rich precipitates.
The resulting Zr-rich precipitates will be fine, coherent, and dispersed throughout the primary BCC matrix.
Zr-rich precipitates will act as stress concentrators that initiate controlled dislocation movement.
Zr-rich precipitates will impede dislocation pile-up.
The proposed effects on dislocation motion will promote distributed plasticity.
The treatment will improve ductility by approximately 20–30% relative to the untreated baseline.
The treatment will make deformation more uniform under tensile and impact loading.
The treatment will retain yield strength comparable to that of the untreated baseline.
The treatment will preserve impact-induced energy-release characteristics.
The predicted improvement will hold at room temperature and under high-strain-rate conditions typical of energetic structural applications.
The beneficial response is restricted to a narrow Zr-content window of approximately 0.5–2 wt.%.
Outside the proposed Zr-content and operating-condition limits, insufficient precipitation or unwanted secondary phases may occur.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires preservation of impact-induced energy release, but the predicted outcome and measurements refer to impact energy absorption. Absorption and energetic release are not interchangeable metrics, so the proposed experiment does not consistently test the stated energetic requirement.
